rv.q: For all the droll comedy, the end, with its mix of anger, sorrow and hope, is quietly moving.
This funny, heartfelt monologue pointedly pokes fun at the indignities and absurdities of life in occupied Palestine.
Even at just 80 minutes the show slightly outstays its welcome.
The Bridge is a fast-paced, funny and captivating production that astutely connects the gap between warm comedy and sobering reality.
The piece showcases the performer’s trademark blend of stand-up, physical theatre, sharply drawn cartoon cameos, and near-relentless audience interaction to tremendous effect.
Alaa offers a witty and heart-rending tale about family and connection juxtaposed with the bad decisions and broken promises of 20th-century British politicans.
Yet it occasionally becomes too comfortable in its comedic strengths, never quite pushing itself, or its audience, beyond them.
Shehada and Beale pull it off flawlessly, offering a show as gag-packed as any top-shelf comedy.

Alaa Shehada stretches his abilities as actor, writer, and comedian, and alongside his director has shaped something endlessly moving, deeply relatable, and startlingly relevant – both to the world we live in now, and the one we have long tried to ignore.
So much of the show really is as fun as it is shocking, which speaks to the quality of the writing.

Much like his acclaimed debut The Horse of Jenin, the insight into Palestinian life, the worldbuilding and the good humour with which the story is told is what makes The Bridge an entertaining and informative tale, about the hopes and dreams which keep Palestinians moving and looking forward.

The Bridge is a production that demands to be seen, an absolute must in a world where both engaging with the oppression experienced around the world, and retaining our joy and hope for a better future are so, so important.
It’s an evening that raises questions and has a point of view that comes across with power and passion.
This is a vital, deeply moving, and uproariously funny night of theatre that you really shouldn't miss.

cn.t: Shehada's one-man show skillfully balances humor and pathos, finding comedy in the bureaucratic absurdities of Palestinian border crossing while delivering pointed political commentary. Critics praise his charismatic performance and the show's tonal control.
